title: GIDEON HAD MANY WIVES AND SEVENTY SONS—PLUS A CONCUBINE IN SHECHEM
paragraphs: GIDEON HAD MANY WIVES AND SEVENTY SONS—PLUS A CONCUBINE IN SHECHEM
The Bible Doesn't Hide What Happened After Gideon's Greatest Victory—and Neither Should We
Everybody remembers the fleece.
Everybody remembers the 300 men.

Everybody remembers the torches, the jars, the trumpets, the terrified Midianite army, and the impossible victory God gave to a frightened man who once asked, “If the LORD be with us, why then is all this befallen us?”
But almost nobody talks about what happened after Gideon became famous.
And maybe that is because Judges 8 becomes uncomfortable.
Very uncomfortable.
Because the man who once hid from Midian in a winepress eventually became one of the most powerful men in Israel.
The man who needed reassurance from God became the man surrounded by influence, wealth, wives, children, and honor.
And buried near the end of his story is a sentence many believers have probably read too quickly:
“And Gideon had threescore and ten sons of his body begotten: for he had many wives. And his concubine that was in Shechem, she also bare him a son, whose name he called Abimelech.”
Judges 8:30–31, KJV.
Seventy sons.
Many wives.
And another woman in Shechem—a concubine—who bore him a son.
Abimelech.
That name matters.
Keep reading.
Because before this story is over, blood will run across a stone.
Brothers will die.
A family will implode.
And one uncomfortable truth will emerge from Gideon’s story:
Sometimes the greatest danger to your soul does not arrive while you are fighting for your life.
Sometimes it arrives after you win.
The Hebrew refuses to soften what happened.
Judges 8:30 says:
“וּלְגִדְעוֹן, הָיוּ שִׁבְעִים בָּנִים, יֹצְאֵי, יְרֵכוֹ: כִּי־נָשִׁים רַבּוֹת, הָיוּ לוֹ”
“Ule-Gid'on hayu shiv'im banim… ki-nashim rabbot hayu lo.”
In straightforward sense:
Gideon had seventy sons who came from him, because he had many wives.
Then verse 31 says:
“וּפִילַגְשׁוֹ אֲשֶׁר בִּשְׁכֶם, יָלְדָה־לּוֹ גַם־הִיא בֵּן; וַיָּשֶׂם אֶת־שְׁמוֹ, אֲבִימֶלֶךְ”
“Ufilagsho asher bi-Shekhem… vayasem et-shemo Avimelekh.”
His concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he gave him the name Abimelech.
The Hebrew word פִּילֶגֶשׁ—pilegesh—means a concubine, a woman in a recognized but lower-status marital or domestic relationship than a primary wife in that ancient social setting.
And Scripture does not interrupt the story to say, “Gideon did this, therefore God approves of this.”
That is not how biblical narrative works.
The Bible often tells us what people did without telling us to imitate what they did.
That distinction matters.
Description is not automatically prescription.
The Bible records Abraham's failures without commanding them.
It records David's adultery without approving it.
It records Solomon's many wives while explicitly showing the spiritual catastrophe associated with them.
And Judges records Gideon honestly.
No public-relations department.
No polished biography.
No attempt to protect the reputation of one of Israel's celebrated deliverers.
That should tell you something beautiful about Scripture.
The Bible is not a museum filled with statues of flawless people.
It is the testimony of a holy God working among desperately flawed human beings.
And that means there may be hope for you.
Because Gideon's story did not begin with a fearless warrior.
It began with a frightened man.
When the angel of the LORD encountered Gideon in Judges 6, Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress, trying to keep it hidden from Midian.
Imagine the scene.
Dust in the air.
Shoulders tense.
Eyes constantly checking the horizon.
Israel had been crushed so severely that people made hiding places in mountains and caves.
Then heaven addresses this frightened man with words that must have sounded almost absurd:
“The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour.”
God was speaking to something Gideon could not yet see in himself.
And some of you understand that.
You know what it is to love God while still being afraid.
To pray while questioning.
To worship while wondering why God has allowed something painful.
To believe and still whisper, “Lord, are You really here?”
Gideon knew that tension.
He asked questions.
He requested signs.
He put out the fleece.
And God patiently dealt with him.
Eventually, Gideon marched into battle with an army God intentionally reduced.
Thousands became hundreds.
Because God was going to make one thing unmistakable:
Israel's salvation would not come from human strength.
The victory belonged to the LORD.
Three hundred men.
Trumpets.
Jars.
Torches.
And God shattered Midian's power.
It is magnificent.
It is cinematic.
It is the part we preach.
But Judges does not end Gideon's biography at the victory celebration.
And neither should we.
Because winning a battle does not mean you have finished guarding your heart.
In fact, success can expose things suffering kept buried.
When you have nothing, dependence on God can feel natural.
When you have influence, money, admiration, authority, options, and people applauding your name...
something changes.
After Gideon's victory, Israel approached him with an extraordinary offer.
They wanted Gideon to rule over them.
Not merely Gideon.
His son.
And his son's son.
A dynasty.
Gideon answered magnificently:
“I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the LORD shall rule over you.”
Judges 8:23.
Beautiful words.
But then the story becomes complicated.
Gideon requested gold from the spoil.
The people willingly gave it.
He made an ephod.
And Judges 8:27 says that Israel went astray after it and that it became “a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.”
Read those final words again.
“To Gideon, and to his house.”
The Midianites could not destroy Gideon's house.
But a snare could enter after the victory.
Then comes the wealth.
Then the many wives.
Then seventy sons.
Then the concubine in Shechem.
Then Abimelech.
And there is an irony in that name that is difficult to ignore.
Avimelekh is built from Hebrew words associated with “father” and “king,” commonly understood as “my father is king” or “father is king.”
Yet Gideon had said:
“I will not rule over you.”
He verbally rejected kingship.
But the world surrounding his later life begins to look remarkably royal.
Many wives.
An enormous household.
Great wealth.
Prestige.
Seventy sons.
And a son named Abimelech.
We should be careful not to claim more than Scripture explicitly tells us about Gideon's motives. The text does not open his mind and tell us precisely why he chose that name.
But the narrative tension is there.
And then Gideon dies.
The great warrior is buried.
The crowds disappear.
The stories remain.
And the consequences keep walking.
Abimelech goes to Shechem.
He appeals to his mother's relatives.
He asks them, essentially, whether they would rather be ruled by Gideon's seventy sons or by one man who is their own flesh and blood.
Money is given to him from the temple of Baal-Berith.
Abimelech hires reckless men.
Then he travels to Ophrah.
To his father's house.
To the place connected with Gideon's legacy.
And there, Judges 9 records one of the darkest scenes in the book.
Abimelech murders his brothers.
On one stone.
The sons of Gideon.
His own brothers.
One after another.
Only Jotham, the youngest, escapes.
Think about that.
The family of the man who defeated Midian was devastated from inside itself.
Gideon defeated an army with 300 men.
Yet after his death, his household became the scene of horrifying violence.
That should shake us.
Because you can win publicly and still neglect something privately.
You can be used by God and still need to guard your heart.
You can have yesterday's testimony and still need today's obedience.
You can destroy an altar to Baal in Judges 6 and later make something that becomes a spiritual snare in Judges 8.
Yesterday's obedience does not give us permission to coast today.
Yesterday's anointing is not a substitute for today's surrender.
And maybe this is where Gideon's story stops being ancient history and starts reading your mail.
Because perhaps your Midian has already fallen.
Maybe God answered the prayer.
Maybe you got the job.
Maybe the business grew.
Maybe people finally noticed you.
Maybe the relationship happened.
Maybe your ministry expanded.
Maybe your page gained followers.
Maybe people started listening when you spoke.
Maybe you survived the season you thought would kill you.
And strangely...
you prayed more when you were desperate.
You searched Scripture more when you were hurting.
You cried before God more when there was nothing in your bank account.
You depended upon Him when every door was closed.
Then the doors opened.
And somewhere between survival and success, something changed.
Not dramatically.
Quietly.
Prayer became shorter.
Conviction became negotiable.
Compromise became explainable.
What once disturbed you became normal.
You still knew Christian language.
You still remembered the testimonies.
You could still tell everyone what God had done.
But the heart that once trembled before Him had started getting comfortable.
That may be the frightening lesson buried inside Gideon's ending.
You do not only need God in the winepress.
You need Him after Midian falls.
You need Jesus when you are poor.
You need Jesus when you prosper.
You need Jesus when nobody knows your name.
You need Jesus when thousands recognize it.
You need Jesus when you are afraid.
You need Jesus when you finally feel powerful.
Especially then.
Because the Gospel is not merely God's method for getting weak people through difficult seasons.
Jesus Christ is our life.
Our righteousness.
Our King.
Our hope.
Our forgiveness.
Our rescue.
Gideon could save Israel temporarily from Midian.
But Gideon could not save Gideon from Gideon.
And neither can you save yourself from yourself.
That is why we need a better Deliverer.
Not merely another judge.
Not another warrior.
Not another inspirational leader.
We need Jesus Christ.
Gideon entered battle with 300 men and emerged victorious.
Jesus walked toward Calvary while His disciples scattered.
Gideon shattered jars and enemies fled.
Jesus allowed His own body to be wounded.
Gideon returned from battle carrying the prestige of victory.
Jesus was mocked, stripped, beaten, crowned with thorns, and nailed to a Roman cross.
Gideon's later household became marked by rivalry and bloodshed.
Jesus shed His own blood to create a redeemed family from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation.
Gideon said the LORD should rule Israel.
Jesus Christ is the King whose reign never ends.
And unlike every human hero in Scripture, Jesus does not need His biography edited.
There is no secret chapter where Christ becomes corrupted by success.
No hidden scandal.
No moral collapse.
No private contradiction waiting to destroy His public righteousness.
He was tempted, yet without sin.
He obeyed the Father perfectly.
He went to the cross willingly.
And there He carried the judgment sinners deserve.
This is where the story turns toward you.
Because perhaps you have your own Judges 8.
Something you do not put in the testimony.
Something after the victory.
Something behind the Christian vocabulary.
Maybe nobody knows.
The private messages.
The addiction.
The affair.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The secret relationship.
The money.
The pride.
The resentment.
The compromise you keep renaming because calling it sin would require repentance.
Maybe you have become very good at remembering what God did through you while avoiding what God is confronting within you.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not die only for the version of you everyone admires.
He died for sinners.
Real sinners.
People with chapters they wish could be ripped from the book.
People who have failed after victories.
People who knew better.
People who compromised.
People who wandered.
People who discovered that defeating an external enemy is sometimes easier than confronting the rebellion inside their own hearts.
And the answer is not hiding.
The answer is repentance.
Not religious performance.
Not pretending.
Not “I'll fix myself first and then come back.”
Come to Christ.
Confess.
Turn.
Bring the darkness into His light.
The cross is where scandal meets grace.
Not cheap grace that calls evil good.
Grace that tells the truth about sin and then announces that the blood of Jesus is sufficient to cleanse the sinner who comes to Him.
That is the Gospel.
Your worst chapter does not become righteous because you explain it.
Your sin does not become harmless because other Christians have done worse.
But your sin does not have to write the final sentence either.
Jesus can.
Maybe that is exactly why you found this article.
Not because you needed another shocking Bible fact about Gideon's wives.
Maybe God is putting His finger on your Judges 8.
The thing after your testimony.
The compromise after your victory.
The idol made from something that once looked like blessing.
The hidden relationship.
The quiet pride.
The secret appetite.
The place where you have been saying, “The LORD shall rule,” while living as though something else already does.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected, didn't it?
If God exposed something while you were reading this, do not run from Him.
Run to Christ.
Not because typing a phrase saves anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not the only believer fighting their way back toward the light.
Not as an algorithm trick.
Somebody you love may be smiling publicly while losing a war privately.
Somebody may be one honest encounter with Scripture away from repentance.
Send this to your family.
Send it to the struggling Christian.
Send it to the person who stopped attending church.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks the Bible sanitizes its heroes, because one extraordinary mark of Scripture is how relentlessly honest it is about human failure.
You may need it again when success starts whispering that you no longer need the dependence that carried you through suffering.
Biblical generosity comes from a willing heart responding to God's grace.
But ministry does require real resources.
Research takes time.
Writing takes time.
Books and discipleship materials take resources.
Reaching more people requires support.
Think of it as voluntary ministry support—an offering of generosity, not a transaction with God and not a replacement for obedience to however Scripture and your conscience direct your giving.
And there is another way to support the mission that costs absolutely nothing:
Share.
One share can enter a home we cannot enter.
One share can reach an old friend at 2:00 in the morning.
One share can land before somebody sitting alone wondering whether God could possibly forgive what they have done.
You may never know what God does with it.
But you can put truth within reach.
We want Scripture opened.
We want Christ proclaimed.
We want wounded believers strengthened.
We want wandering hearts called home.
We want people who have spent years hiding to discover that repentance is not the doorway into humiliation—it is the doorway back into the light.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite the lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not believe yet.
Jesus is calling sinners home.
That invitation costs you nothing because it cost Him everything.
Gideon's story warns us not to confuse being used by God with being beyond the need for God.
Not every hero finishes every chapter heroically.
Not every victory guarantees faithfulness tomorrow.
And perhaps the most dangerous moment in your spiritual life will not be when you are trembling in the winepress.
Perhaps it will be when the battle is over...
the applause is loud...
the gold is accumulating...
the doors are opening...
and you slowly forget Who gave you the victory.
So guard your heart.
Stay near the cross.
Stay humble.
Stay repentant.
Stay in Scripture.
Do not build an idol out of yesterday's blessing.
Do not let yesterday's testimony become today's excuse.
And if you have already wandered...
come home.
If your story contains things you are ashamed to admit...
come home.
If you have been living two lives...
come home.
If you won battles publicly and lost yourself privately...
come home.
Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
His blood is still sufficient.
His grace is still greater than your shame.
His resurrection still announces that death does not get the final word.
And your scandal does not have to write your ending.
The stone in Judges 9 became a place where brothers died.
But centuries later, another stone would be rolled away from another place of death.
And the empty tomb would announce to every broken Gideon, every wandering believer, every ashamed sinner, every exhausted soul, and every person convinced their story is already ruined:
Jesus Christ is alive.
Grace still rewrites stories.
What is happening in my heart after the victory?
Then give Jesus the honest answer.
Because the chapter you're most ashamed of may become the very place where you finally discover how astonishing His grace really is.
